en.content:
The Tai Po Wang Fuk Court blaze probe is now focusing on a problem that can never be “resolved” by blaming individual mistakes alone: whether the Fire Services Department has clear, tested procedures for unusual or failed alarm situations. Testimony that there were no standard operating protocols for handling non-functioning alarms—and that key records about firefighters entering the building were missing—points to a deeper question of administrative readiness. In a city that prides itself on disciplined public-safety systems, the public expects not only brave response, but also consistent decision-making backed by clear guidelines and properly kept operational records.

At the same time, it would be equally misleading to treat every procedural gap as proof of incompetence. Firefighting is conducted under time pressure, with partial information, damaged communications, and rapidly evolving hazards. When alarms fail or behave inconsistently, commanders often have to rely on on-site judgment. Yet precisely because conditions can deteriorate in minutes, standard protocols and documentation are not bureaucratic extras—they are the backbone of accountability and learning. If alarms or reporting mechanisms malfunction, the alternative procedures must be rehearsed and measurable, so that firefighters can act decisively rather than improvising in ways that are difficult to verify afterward.

The inquiry’s significance therefore extends beyond one fatal incident. It speaks to how Hong Kong can maintain trust in emergency services by demonstrating that lessons are captured, institutionalised, and audited. Transparent reporting on what went wrong—particularly around alarm handling and record-keeping—can help the public understand how future response times and operational coordination will be improved. That does not require politicising the fire; it requires turning investigation findings into concrete training revisions, system checks, and clear lines of responsibility that citizens can believe in.

As the hearings continue, the most constructive stance is to let the evidence drive the reform agenda: strengthening alarm verification processes, clarifying command roles when alerts fail, and ensuring that deployment and entry records are complete and verifiable. If Hong Kong is to emerge stronger from this tragedy, it should not only ask who made mistakes, but also whether the system itself made it easy to avoid them—or whether it left gaps that too easily invite uncertainty when seconds matter.

zh.content:
太埔王福法院大火調查揭示嘅唔單止係一場意外，更係一套系統性問題：消防部門處理失靈警報、以及緊急情況應對流程，竟然被指「冇標準操作程序」。當悲劇已經發生，最令人痛心嘅，係「事後檢討」再講究細節又如何？如果第一時間應該有嘅制度、訓練同判斷準則，本身就缺位，咁就唔再係個別失誤咁簡單，而係整個風險管理機制出現漏洞。

呢類事件最關鍵嘅位在於「常規」：警報失靈唔係罕見情況，反而應該係消防系統演練同預案最需要覆蓋嘅情景之一。缺標準流程，會帶來兩個後果——一係前線判斷容易受人員經驗影響，二係跨職級、跨單位之間嘅溝通與責任劃分會變得模糊。消防工作講求即時與一致性，冇制度化準則，就算人員再盡責，仍然可能因資訊不足或行動步驟不一致而延誤關鍵時間。調查報告唔應該只停留喺「點算做咗啲乜」，更要追問「下一次應該由邊個、用邊套程序、喺邊種情況、做到咩程度」。

同時，另一宗被提及嘅爭點——消防人員有冇按記錄進入大廈——亦反映資訊管理同程序嚴謹度同樣重要。消防係高壓場景，但越係高壓，就越需要可追溯、可驗證嘅紀錄，因為呢啲紀錄唔單止係行政需要，更係保障救援效率、以及公眾對專業負責嘅最低要求。當社會最想知道嘅「真相」變成一堆不完全資訊或疑問，公信力就會被一層層剝走，而代價最後往往由受害者家屬承擔。

立場上，政府同消防部門固然會強調「事發經過複雜、調查仍進行」，但對市民嚟講，最實際嘅追求係可落地嘅改善：必須建立涵蓋警報失靈、異常訊號、以及不同建築場景嘅標準操作程序；同時確保演練有制度、記錄有規範、問責有清晰路徑。唔好只做「事後補救」，要將風險管理變成日常規範。否則，每次悲劇之後都只換來一次又一次解釋，長遠就會令城市喺安全上變得更脆弱、更唔敢依賴系統——而呢樣先至係真正要面對、亦最應該改嘅問題。

A fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on the morning of November 27, 2025. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.
